sections.h: Saul in Acts 8–9: persecutor, called, hunted
sections.b: Acts introduces Saul as the man who approved Stephen's death and then "mauled" the church, dragging believers from their homes (Acts 8:1–3). On the road to Damascus with the high priest's letters, he is thrown down by light from heaven and hears Jesus ask why Saul is persecuting him (Acts 9:1–9). Ananias, sent in a vision, lays hands on him and learns that Saul is a "vessel" chosen to carry Jesus' name to Gentiles, kings and Israelites, and to suffer for it (Acts 9:15–16). Saul preaches at once in the synagogues of Damascus, escapes a plot over the wall in a basket (compare 2 Corinthians 11:32–33), is vouched for in Jerusalem by Barnabas, and is sent home to Tarsus (Acts 9:19–30). Luke's account compresses what Paul tells in Galatians 1:13–24 and differs from it on the stay in Arabia and on whom Saul met in Jerusalem.

common: Paul's experience on the Damascus road is the most famous conversion in history.
Paul was not renamed at his conversion; Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul his Roman one.
uncommon: Some scholars, following Krister Stendahl, think "call" describes the Damascus event better than "conversion," since Paul never left Israel's God.

sections.b: The first mission outside Jerusalem goes to the Samaritans. Philip, one of the Seven, announces the Messiah in "the city of Samaria," with healings, exorcisms and great joy; many are baptized, among them the magician Simon (Acts 8:4–13). Peter and John come from Jerusalem and lay hands on the believers, who receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14–17), and on the way home they tell the good news in many Samaritan villages (Acts 8:25). John, who once wanted fire to fall on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:52–55), now prays for Samaritans to receive the Spirit. The mission fulfills the second stage of Jesus' command in Acts 1:8. Since Samaritans hoped for a prophet like Moses rather than a son of David, Philip's "Messiah" met a hope shaped by Deuteronomy 18:15.
sections.refs: Acts 1:8; Acts 8:4–25; Acts 9:31; Luke 9:52–55; Luke 17:16; John 4:39–42; Deuteronomy 18:15

sections.b: Simon, a magician who had astounded Samaria and was hailed as "the Power of God, the one called Great," believed Philip's preaching and was baptized (Acts 8:9–13). When he saw the Spirit given through the apostles' hands, he offered money for the same authority, and Peter cursed his silver and called him to repent (Acts 8:18–24). The church named the buying of spiritual office "simony" after him. Second-century writers turned Simon into the founder of heresy: Justin Martyr says he was honored as a god at Rome (First Apology 26), Irenaeus makes him the father of the Gnostics (Against Heresies 1.23), and the Acts of Peter tells of his fatal flight over Rome. These stories go far beyond Acts, which leaves Simon asking for prayer.

uncommon: Some scholars think the title "the Great Power" was a Samaritan name for God, so that the crowds took Simon as God's presence on earth.

sections.h: The Spirit in Acts 8–10: three different orders
sections.b: In Samaria baptized believers receive the Spirit only when Peter and John lay hands on them (Acts 8:14–17). Saul is to be filled with the Spirit when Ananias lays hands on him, and then he is baptized (Acts 9:17–18). At Caesarea the Spirit falls on Cornelius' household while Peter is still speaking, before any baptism, and they speak in tongues (Acts 10:44–48), which Peter later compares to Pentecost (Acts 11:15–17). The variety has been read as Luke recording God's freedom in new situations, as exceptions to the norm of Acts 2:38, as evidence of a later Spirit baptism (Pentecostal teaching), or as the root of confirmation (Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican teaching). See the cards at Acts 8 and Acts 19.

Samaritan men and women are baptized "into the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 8:12, 16). The Ethiopian eunuch asks, "What is stopping me from being baptized?", and he and Philip go down into the water (Acts 8:36–38); a very old addition, the KJV's 8:37, gives him a confession of faith first. Saul is baptized as soon as his sight returns (Acts 9:18). Cornelius' household is baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ" after the Spirit has already fallen on them, because no one can "stop" it (Acts 10:47–48). These passages are central to debates about believers' baptism, the mode of baptism and the relation of baptism to the Spirit (see the card at Acts 8:38).

common: The eunuch's question "What is stopping me?" has been read as an early baptismal formula (Oscar Cullmann).

sections.b: Acts 8:26–39 tells of a eunuch, the finance minister of the Kandake, queen of Kush, riding home from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah 53. Philip explains the passage as speaking of Jesus, and the man asks to be baptized. A man whom Deuteronomy 23:1 kept out of the assembly finds no barrier in the church, and Isaiah's promise to eunuchs, "a marker and a name / that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5), comes true. Early writers say he went home to preach (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.23.2; Eusebius, Church History 2.1.13).

sections.h: An official of the queen of Kush
sections.b: The "Ethiopian" of Acts 8:27 came from Kush, the Nile kingdom ruled from Meroë in what is now Sudan, whose queens bore the title Kandake. He is the first person from Africa south of Egypt baptized in the New Testament, and his story was read as the fulfillment of Psalm 68:31: "Cush will run to stretch out its hands to God" (Psalm 68:31). The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church honors him as the first evangelist of its land, though the court of Aksum became Christian through Frumentius in the 300s.

Acts 8:32–33 quotes Isaiah 53:7–8 in the Greek of the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew, especially in 53:8 ("Who will tell of his generation?"). The eunuch asks whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else, the question Jewish and Christian readers have long debated, and Philip begins from that passage to tell him about Jesus (Acts 8:35). The quotation stops just before the lines about the servant bearing the people's sins, which some scholars take as a sign that Luke stresses the innocent suffering and vindication of the servant more than an atoning death; others think the whole passage is meant.

Cornelius, a centurion at Caesarea, was a God-fearer: a Gentile who prayed to Israel's God and gave to the poor of Israel without being circumcised (Acts 10:1–2). Guided by matching visions, Peter enters his house, though Jewish custom avoided it, and declares that "in every nation the one who fears him and practices righteousness is welcome to him" (Acts 10:35). The Holy Spirit falls on the household before baptism, and Peter has them baptized (Acts 10:44–48). Luke tells the story three times (Acts 10; 11:1–18; 15:7–11) because it settled that Gentiles belong to God's people without becoming Jews. The Ethiopian eunuch, a little earlier, may also have been a Gentile worshiper (Acts 8:27).

uncommon: A. T. Kraabel argued that Luke invented the "God-fearers" as a class; the Aphrodisias inscription (published 1987) persuaded most scholars that they existed.

sections.b: On a roof in Joppa the hungry Peter sees a sheet full of every kind of animal and hears, "Get up, Peter; kill and eat." He refuses, as faithful Jews had refused unclean food since the Maccabean martyrs: "I have never eaten anything common and unclean." The voice answers, "What God has made clean, you must not call common," three times (Acts 10:13–16). Peter applies the vision to people: he must not call any human being common or unclean (Acts 10:28). Most Christians read it as ending the food laws as well, with Mark 7:19 and Romans 14:14; some Messianic Jews and Seventh-day Adventists hold that it concerns people only.
sections.refs: Acts 10:9–16; Acts 10:28; Acts 11:5–10; Leviticus 11; 1 Maccabees 1:62–63; Ezekiel 4:14; Mark 7:19; Romans 14:14

sections.b: Peter uses two words: akathartos, "unclean," the Law's word for forbidden animals, and koinos, "common," for what is ordinary or made impure by contact (Acts 10:14). He has just lodged with a tanner, whose trade with animal carcasses made him often unclean (Acts 9:43). Entering a Gentile's house was avoided by custom, not by any law of Moses, since some held Gentile dwellings to be unclean (Mishnah Oholot 18:7); Peter says God has shown him to call no person common or unclean (Acts 10:28).
sections.refs: Acts 9:43; Acts 10:14–15; Acts 10:28; Acts 11:2–3; Leviticus 11:39–40; Leviticus 20:24–26

sections.b: Acts 9–10 is full of hospitality: Peter lodges with Simon the tanner (Acts 9:43), takes Cornelius' Gentile messengers in as his guests (Acts 10:23), enters Cornelius' house (Acts 10:27–28) and stays on for some days (Acts 10:48). The complaint in Jerusalem is precisely that he "ate with" uncircumcised men (Acts 11:3). Sharing roof and table was where the line between Jew and Gentile was felt most, and where the church first crossed it.
sections.refs: Acts 9:43; Acts 10:6; Acts 10:23; Acts 10:48; Acts 11:3; Galatians 2:11–14

sections.b: Two people in Acts 9–10 are known for their alms. Tabitha of Joppa was "full of good works and of the alms she gave" and made clothes for widows (Acts 9:36–39). Cornelius, a Gentile, gave many gifts to the poor of Israel, and an angel tells him his prayers and alms have gone up before God "as a remembrance," like the token portion of an offering (Acts 10:2–4, 31; Leviticus 2:2). Luke shares the Jewish esteem for almsgiving seen in Tobit 12:9.
sections.refs: Acts 9:36–39; Acts 10:2–4; Acts 10:31; Tobit 12:8–12; Leviticus 2:2; Luke 11:41

sections.b: When Tabitha died, "all the widows" stood weeping around Peter, showing the tunics and cloaks she had made for them (Acts 9:39). She seems to have been their patron, and after raising her Peter calls in "the saints and the widows" (Acts 9:41) and stands her before them alive, as though the widows were a recognized group in the church, as in Acts 6:1 and 1 Timothy 5:3–16.

Peter sends the mourners out, kneels and prays, and says, "Tabitha, get up" (Acts 9:40), almost the words of Jesus to Jairus' daughter, "Talitha koum" (Mark 5:41). The raising echoes Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:32–37). Like those raisings it is a return to ordinary life, not the resurrection body; but it shows the risen Lord's power at work, and many in Joppa come to believe. In Cornelius' house Peter's witness to the resurrection rests on having eaten and drunk with the risen Jesus (Acts 10:40–41).

sections.h: Peter in Samaria, Lydda, Joppa and Caesarea
sections.b: Peter, with John, confirms the Samaritan mission and confronts Simon the magician (Acts 8:14–25). On a tour of the churches he heals Aeneas at Lydda and raises Tabitha at Joppa, as Jesus had done (Acts 9:32–42). At Joppa, the port Jonah sailed from, the son of Jonah (Matthew 16:17) is called by a vision to a Gentile house, protests "Not at all, Lord!", and goes (Acts 10). His sermon there is a Gospel in miniature (Acts 10:34–43), and his question "Surely no one can hold back the water?" opens the church to Gentiles (Acts 10:47).

Luke twice tells of two people given matching visions so that they will meet: Saul sees Ananias coming while Ananias is told to go to Saul (Acts 9:10–12), and Cornelius sees an angel while Peter, in a trance, sees the sheet of animals (Acts 10:3–16). Ancient readers knew such "double dreams" from other literature as a sign that the gods arranged a meeting; Luke uses the form to show that the mission to Saul and to the Gentiles was God's own work.

Peter twice describes the crucifixion as hanging Jesus "on a tree" (Acts 5:30; 10:39), language drawn from Deuteronomy 21:22–23, "for a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23). The phrase admits the scandal that a crucified Messiah seemed accursed, and the apostles answer it with the resurrection: God raised him on the third day (Acts 10:40). Paul draws the same line in Galatians 3:13.
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39–40; Acts 13:29; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24

sections.b: The KJV's Acts 8:37, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God," is absent from every early Greek manuscript and from the Byzantine majority, but Irenaeus knew it about AD 180. It probably came from the baptismal practice of the second-century church. Erasmus put it into the printed Greek New Testament from the margin of a manuscript, and so it entered the Textus Receptus and the KJV. Modern Bibles leave the number 37 empty. Other changes to Acts 8–10 in the Textus Receptus ("hard for thee to kick against the pricks" at 9:5–6) were translated by Erasmus from the Latin.

Cornelius' household spoke in tongues and declared God's greatness when the Spirit fell on them, the sign that convinced Peter's Jewish companions that Gentiles had received "the same gift" as the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 10:45–46; Acts 11:17). Pentecostal teaching reads this verse with Acts 2:4 and 19:6 as showing tongues to be the first sign of baptism in the Spirit; other churches see tongues as one gift among many (1 Corinthians 12:30).
sections.refs: Acts 2:4; Acts 10:44–46; Acts 11:15–17; Acts 19:6; 1 Corinthians 12:10; 1 Corinthians 12:30

sections.b: Luke says "the Jews" of Damascus plotted to kill Saul (Acts 9:23), where Paul himself names the ethnarch of King Aretas (2 Corinthians 11:32), and the Hellenists of Jerusalem tried to kill him (Acts 9:29). The phrase means local Jewish leaders and groups, not the Jewish people; the believers in these stories (Ananias, Peter, the disciples) are Jews too. In a Gentile house Peter says "they" killed Jesus (Acts 10:39), not "you," and Cornelius is praised for being well spoken of by "the whole Jewish nation" (Acts 10:22).
